no, as it would materially help the Winnipeg committee to know what they can expect from Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It is obvious that any such action as that would have to be of general application all over Canada. The province of Saskatchewan are doing this very thing themselves in conjunction with their cities. The province of Quebec has adopted another method of encouraging the return to the farm lands of that province. With respect to the other provinces I am not presently acquainted with what they are doing. I am not yet prepared to agree that this is primarily a responsibility of the dominion. As I said in my observations an hour or so ago, many schemes have been started. I have investigated a lot of them, and I must say that while they were started undoubtedly with the best of intentions. they could not hope to go forward with any degree of success because the people who started them were more enthusiastic about the theory than thejr were acquainted, in my view, with the actual facts of how to assist people on to the land. It strikes me that to be a. successful farmer, and I say this subject to correction bj' any of those who have spent their lives on the land, you require a good deal of training to know how to make headway on a farm, and of course everyone will agree with me that you also need an abundance of courage. I think it would be a great mistake just to take people who happen to be unemployed and put them on a farm. I think no useful purpose would be served, and one season would not pass before they would forget even to thank us for our efforts. I believe they must have the desire to go on the land and must have some agricultural background. True, an odd one who has not had experience may succeed, but from my talks with men who should know-and I believe, do know-I learn it is most essential that we do not take people who are utterly inexperienced, and put them out on the land. They would suffer great hardships.
In the judgment of the minister, any relief assistance granted by the Dominion government could not be diverted to help any scheme of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The subject has been given a great deal of consideration. I do not wish to appear to be one who is not prepared to put forth every effort to help as much as possible. I do not think however that time has yet arrived-and I hope it will not arrive-when in Canada we have to begin a system of state-aided colonization. The other phase of the matter has a good deal of merit,
[Mr. Woodsworth.J
namely to capitalize what we know we might have to pay to a certain person for purposes of direct relief, and help to establish him on a farm. If the provinces cannot discharge their legislative responsibilities, and find themselves hopelessly insolvent-I hope none of them do, and I believe they are not in that position- then they may make out a case whereby the federal government would be justified in adopting throughout Canada a plan such as that suggested by the hon. member.

As I said earlier, I am sorry to be so insistent. The committee in Winnipeg knows perfectly well that if the scheme is to go through this year it must be proceeded with within the next few days. We have had warm weather in Winnipeg, and they are urging the government to give the necessary yes or no with regard to their proposition for the present season. * I ask the minister just to say yes or no; with whatever he says I shall be quite satisfied. I should like however to have a direct answer which would enable the committee in Winnipeg to know what it may expect from the government.

Representing one of the Winnipeg constituencies, I was deeply interested in the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) and I heartily support the principle put forward by him. In the matter of unemployment Winnipeg has a burden upon its shoulders which is daily becoming more unbearable. In that city the idea of assisting to relieve the unemployed by putting them on the land has received a good deal of consideration. As I understand it there is no suggestion indiscriminately to place upon the land people without any agricultural background. In the city of Winnipeg, however, as in many other centres throughout Canada, there are people who in more prosperous days, for one reason or another, picked up their belongings and moved from the rural to the urban centres. What caused them to do so is not of importance, but the fact is that many unemployed in the city of Winnipeg-and I know it-are experienced agriculturists and, having found that the bright lights of the city are not as wonderful as they had thought, are now hungry to go back to the land.
I do not think the present is the time to debate whether or not the duty is primarily that of the federal government, the provincial government or the administration in the city of Winnipeg. We are faced with certain given facts, and we know that since the special session of 1930 the federal government has

seen fit to cooperate not only in principle but with funds to relieve the unemployment situation through public works undertakings and payments of direct relief. If the federal government has funds to assist in the erection of buildings in the city of Winnipeg, if it can expend federal moneys for food, clothing and fuel to effect direct relief, then there is no technical reason why funds could not be provided to place unemployed men on the land, if it is deemed expedient so to do.
I urge upon the serious consideration of the minister the facts brought out so forcibly by the hon. member for St. Boniface, and the suggestion that the- government seriously consider endeavouring to work out a plan along the line suggested iby the hon. member. It is my understanding that before prorogation there will be introduced such further legislation as may be necessary to deal with unemployment. It is not for me to say, nor do I know what the nature of that legislation will be. However the public press carries information, or what purports to be information, to the effect that the relief granted will be confined to what is known as direct relief. In my opinion it would be deplorable if relief were confined to direct relief.
Hear, hear.

I hope such will not be the case, but that whatever legislation is introduced in the house will be sufficiently wide that the measure of aid to be granted will not be confined to direct relief. In that connection it is my hope that in working out the relief scheme this matter of placing those who are well qualified and anxious and hungry to go on the land will be fitted into the program. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) asked: Where would they get the farms? That situation has been canvassed. I know that in the province of Manitoba there are many abandoned farms. There is no suggestion of putting people out into the wilderness or the bush; abandoned farms are available. Many of them are available because of abandonment which took place as a result of the soldiers' settlement scheme. Farms were bought at a price far beyond their intrinsic value, with the result that there have come back to the municipalities farms which were once well cultivated, and with substantial buildings situated thereon. Titles to them have reverted either to the municipalities, for taxes, or to the crown. They are improved; the buildings are going to ruin, and the land-and it is good land- is growing up with weeds. Certainly there is a tremendous economic waste. The suggestion has been made that under the proposed settlement scheme these lands might be carefully selected and be made availaible at a mere nominal value. If they were given by the municipality or by the crown to the individuals placed thereon, to my mind that in itself would be a good investment. They would then become productive, which would mean revenue to the municipalities in which they were located. I have very great pleasure in taking advantage of this opportunity to urge strongly upon the minister the advisability of keeping an open mind on that question and endeavouring to work it out.
Would you have the government equip these farms?

Let me answer that in this way. I would suggest that in working it out there be a committee, and without casting any reflection upon members of either the legislature of Manitoba or this house I would suggest that the members of the committee be not politicians, not members of either assembly, but practical business men and agriculturists wdio would choose the locations and judge as to the suitability of the individuals desiring to be so placed. With regard to the capital, that could be provided jointly by the governments and the municipalities, as has been done in the matter of direct relief. This could be done instead of merely supplying a man with food and lodging; it would give him a stake and a real chance. Even though there were many failures, with a fair percentage of successes the scheme would be worth while. When you give direct relief the relief is only temporary. It seems to me the other system has more vision to it; you are really giving a man a stake in the country.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the suggestion just made, and to many others which have been offered. I had intended to ask a few questions and perhaps make a few comments with regard to land settlement when that item came up, so I shall reserve what I have to say until that time, save this: If a man of fair capacity is placed upon an improved farm, with no capital debt and with a small amount of assistance to start with, I believe it is possible for such a man to make his living. Unquestionably it has been proved to be true in respect of all our assisted colonization attempts, under which we have placed men on farms with fairly heavy capital debts, that from the moment those men were placed they became potential problems, and now they are practically all problems.
With regard to the suggestion just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, if unemployed were placed upon abandoned

farms, without capital charge and with a small sum of money to assist them, at once another tremendous problem would be raised. I refer to the attitude of the soldier settlers, the empire settlers and the civilian settlers who have purchased land from or through the board. You would at once raise the important question as to what was to be done with those who are carrying their debts, and who are now fighting in an endeavour to obtain greater relief. They would point to such a movement as a very real reason why they also should have all their debts cancelled and why they should be treated in the same way. I am not discussing that question at the moment, but this is something which certainly must-be considered in relation to any scheme for placing men on farms without obligation to themselves.

If I understood the
figures correctly, a moment ago the minister said that during last year 14,000 men had been placed on farms. I took the minister's statement to refer to single, hired men. Was that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.
Could the minister tell me what proportion of those 14,000 men were put on farms in old Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I could not say, but in the entire province of Ontario-
Has the minister the figures by counties?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No, but up to April 2,
1932, there were 4.165 men placed in Ontario.
Were those farm hands?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Could the minister
give me some idea of where they were placed in Ontario? At the moment I am interested only in old Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have not that information before me, but I think I can get it and let the hon. member have it by counties.

I thank the minister. With regard to farming under present conditions, when the farm industry is perhaps at its lowest ebb in our history, I want to say that in Ontario to-day you could go up and down the county roads, especially in the western part of the province, where there is land equal to any in the world and where the facilities so far as buildings, machinery and so on are concerned are unsurpassed, and in

many instances you could find farmers who would be very glad to move off the land if they could get someone to assume the burden of the mortgage. In my judgment to go ahead and attempt any back to the land movement in old Ontario would be futile and a sheer waste of money. There have been more sheriff's sales of farms in the last year in Ontario than in any previous ten-year period in our history, and I am surprised that the minister and the government should attempt to work out any back to the land policy at the present time. The drift is the other way; sheriffs are driving a lot of farmers from their homes in Ontario. I -will go further and say that the farmers who are hanging on, hoping that conditions will improve and prices pick up, are remaining on the land because they happened to have some small nest egg laid away for a rainy day, and they are fast approaching the end of those resources. What they will do then I do not know, but I would urge on the minister that he should not enter upon, any back to the land scheme. If the government wants any scheme let them work out some policy that will aid those already on the farms so that at least they can make a living.

As I understand it there
were 14,000 farm hands placed by the department, and in addition there were approximately 30,000 others l-ccated on farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Men, women and children.
I think the figure was somewhere about 6.000 families.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There were 6.352 families.
What form did the assistance given by the government take? Just what did the government do by way of placing them on farms?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
In the fall of 1930 the Department of Immigration and Colonization got in touch with the colonization departments of the two railways. The idea arose from the desire on the part of the government to revoke what was commonly called the railway agreements with respect to immigration. There was some hesitancy on the part of the railways to agree with the restrictions that were impending and were placed upon immigration, but after several conferences lasting a week or so they were content that these agreements be revoked; and out of that last conference came the idea that rather than see the colonization establishments of the railways and of the department dissolved, we should turn their activities towards an endeavour to

Supply-Immigration
colonize people who were then in Canada, who wanted to go back to the land and who had enough money to enable them to do so. A survey was made, as well as one could be made, of the people with money and agricultural experience then in Canada.
IVho made that survey?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It. was made partly by the railways and partly by ourselves through the various land settlement agencies in Canada, with a view to finding out that class of person who had left the farm, attracted no doubt by the high wages that prevailed in industry in past years, but now finding themselves out of employment, their savings going into rents and other expenses of that sort in the cities. Then an effort was made by the two railways and the department to list available suitable farms throughout Canada, and while that survey was not a complete one by any means, yet we assembled that information. The railways and the department interviewed the person desiring to go back to the farm, finding out what kind of farm he wanted.
What facilities has the department to cany on that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It is and has been for several years organized from coast to coast under the land settlement branch.
In eastern Canada also?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

The Soldier Settlement
Boards?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes. These people were placed on the' land as I have indicated. Whether we have done them an injury by assisting them to get back to the land is a matter of opinion, but certainly I am not prepared to agree with that suggestion at all, because I have had too many expressions of satisfaction from those people who have gone on the farms and who are mighty happy to be there, in spite of what the hon. member for South Perth has said. In the province of Ontario 611 families have been placed on farms.

Where were they
placed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have not that information at the moment but I will give it to the hon. gentleman before the estimates are through. That was the policy we pursued. The railways and the department used the existing organizations to bring the prospective farmer into touch with the farms that were
available, and we very carefully went into the question of purchase to see that he did not suffer by reason of making an improvident bargain. So far as that could be avoided, we tried to safeguard him. I went over many of them myself and the officers throughout Canada carefully canvassed the situation, because there are still people who can drive a pretty hard bargain when selling farm lands. I wanted to avoid as far as possible a repetition of what happened in some cases in the earlier days of the Soldier Settlement Board. If the department and the railway companies are, as suggested, totally wrong in this effort, then of course we shall have to suffer for our delinquency; but no one can convince me that we are wrong, because I am persuaded that these people are immeasurably better off where they are now. While a large percentage of them cannot make a considerable amount of money just now, nevertheless they will stay on the land.

There are a large number of people in the city of Quebec who would be only too glad to go on the land, and I should like the minister to indicate the procedure they would have to follow if they wanted to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I am assuming that they are people with some money.
No one in my county has any money left now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I should say that in the city of Quebec they could avail themselves of the assistance granted by the province.
So that it is provincial, so far as Quebec is concerned. That is what I am coming to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is scarcely fair.

If the minister refers to the provincial government my request for information for some of my constituents who would like to go on farms, why has he been talking so much about the 44,000 he placed on farms?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I trust we shall not get into acrimony by reason of misunderstandings. The people I am talking about are people who have some money.
And who could have gone without any assistance from this government at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Not necessarily.

What did the government do for them, then? The minister talks glibly of having made a survey through his land settle-

Let us, if possible, endeavour to segregate the railways from the land settlement organization. If my information is correct,-I have not checked it-I do not think that the land settlement office in Sherbrooke can have a personnel of more than five or six. The minister has said to the house, and very proudly, that the land settlement board has an organization all over Canada, that it was able to list the lands that were for sale, and was able to make a survey of the people in the cities; and, mind you, in the province of Quebec he takes one of the smaller cities as headquarters. I tell him it must have been an impossible task to organize the bade to the land movement in that province through the organization he has in Sherbrooke. It is altogether outside the realm of common sense to think that a few people in the city of Sherbrooke, a small office staff, could make anything like a survey of people in Montreal who are looking for employment. It is impossible for an office staff a hundred miles away, a staff of people who in all probability know nothing about the citizens of Montreal and nothing about agricultural conditions in the province of Quebec, except in so far as they may be acquainted with conditions in the district surrounding Sherbrooke, to make a survey of the people with money in the city of Montreal who would like to go on the land. What do they know about farms in the county

of Kamouraska or in the county of Temis-couata? Would they have the faintest idea of how many vacant farms could be purchased in the county of Rimouski on which people could obtain a living, provided there was not too much of a capital debt before they started? If they are not doing the work properly, why do we talk so much about it? I am rather under the impression that in so far as my province is concerned, the work was done by the railways, and if the minister is frank I think he will admit that that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I will look into it further and if that is true, I shall have no hesitation in saying so.

I appreciate that reply of the minister after the speeches he has made and after the newspapers of this country have been putting him up as the great colonizer, the new father of his country. He has stated he is placing people on the land, but when I ask him how he does it, he says he will look into the matter. If he has not the information surely he should be courteous enough to say, "My deputy has that information, I will ask him and then give the information to the committee." I have no doubt the same situation exists in Ontario. Could the minister inform the committee how many land settlement boards there are in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have not that information but I can easily obtain it.

Does not the minister think that in order to get his estimates through he should obtain this information? We all want to get home but I do not think he should take advantage of that fact to come before the committee without knowing anything about bis department. It is a matter of common courtesy and public policy that a man paid to be a minister should know what he is administering. I have no desire to be offensive to the minister, but I think he should have the information desired by the committee. I can remember years ago hon. members then sitting on this side of the house waxing very indignant at the then Minister of Immigration. The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) one of the most genial of men, was blocked for four or five days in the passing of his simple estimates because it was his first year as minister and he dared to make the statement that he would get certain papers and have them available for the evening.

He was told he was mentally unfit.

No, it was another minister who was told he was mentally unfit. There is nothing attracting more attention throughout the country than this problem of land settlement. It is easy enough to talk of land settlement, but there are many practical difficulties to be overcome before a large number of people can be settled on the land. I should like to see them settled, but before that can be brought about we must have a better organization than the present sketchy system. Placing one single family on the land and putting it in a position to obtain a living is a considerable job. If the minister does not know how that is going to be done, then I suggest to him that he get busy and learn. The cases referred to by the minister may have had some capital, but considerable study must be made of marketing, transportation and other questions and that cannot be done with a staff consisting of four or five people. Again I suggest to the minister that he should be able to give the committee the fullest information on this subject.

Mr. Chairman, I come
from Manitoba and notwithstanding the deprecatory attitude adopted by many hon. members in connection with this movement, I am keenly interested in it. At the present time the city of Winnipeg in cooperation with the province of Manitoba is placing several dozen families, not on farms necessarily, but on parcels of land where they can make their own living. I am fairly certain that an appeal has been made to this government to give some assistance to this movement, and I should like to have an undertaking from the minister that at least he will give this matter serious consideration. A short time ago the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) stated that farmers in Ontario were being forced off their farms. That may be very pitiful, but they at least had a roof over their heads and they have had a living for the last eighteen months or two years when hundreds of thousands of other Canadians have had to get along without. An effort is being made by the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba to place these people beyond the realm of charity, at least for the time being, and, as I said before, I appeal to the minister to undertake to give serious consideration to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That matter is under consideration, and I am sure that the government will be sympathetically inclined to any effort being made to assist the people of Manitoba oi of any other province.

We seem
to be in the position of not knowing what to
do. Some hon. members are recommending one thing while others recommend another. I should like to know if a survey has been made of the provinces in order to find out how many farms would be available. Could the minister advise how many farms at suitable prices have been found to be available for this scheme, say in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: If the committee was considering the proper vote I would have more accurate information available.

Is any money being voted
this year for this particular purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The soldier settlement
vote would cover this matter; we are dealing now with civil government.
Votes numbers 55, 56, 57 and 58 cover the matter which we have been discussing all afternoon.

Last evening the minister
said he would be perfectly willing to discuss this matter under this vote, and knowing that, he should have had the information available this afternoon.

I think the committee has a distinct grievance against the minister in this respect. This matter was discussed to a considerable extent last evening 'and I am surprised that the minister did not bring down the information which he has promised to bring down this evening. It has been stated that 50,000 have been placed on the land, but I am inclined to think that when we receive accurate information it will be found that that number has dwindled considerably.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a good deal of interest this afternoon to the discussion which has taken place, and I have been thinking of how quickly people forget. This country has a very elaborate land settlement scheme- I do not know the exact figures, as I intended to get them from the minister when the particular item was under discussion-which up to date has probably cost $60,000,000.
More than that.

Perhaps
more than that has been paid for this experiment in land settlement. Seventy odd per cent of those placed on the land have been sons of farmers raised on the land. It has been said that too much was paid for the land purchased, but I think the fact is that in 90 per cent of the cases the land was acquired at prevailing prices; in only 10
Supply-Immigration

per cent of the cases could it be said that high prices or some other influence had entered into the transaction. I should like to bolster up the minister a little in his determination not to be let into another scheme of this kind, but I agree with hon. members on this side when they say that he would be well advised not to do too much blowing about having placed people back on the land.
A bit of hot air.

No, I won't say that. I would give the minister a little advice in this connection. The soldier land settlement scheme, to put it mildly, has been a colossal failure. From the moment I took control of the department for a short time I felt it would be so. May I say to my hon. friends from the cities of Winnipeg, Sherbrooke and Quebec that if they want to organize any return to the land movement they had better have a board of practical farmers rather than doctors and lawyers.
Hear, hear.

Let men who have had some experience on the land, and have paid for their experience, advise those who want to try farming. \ou cannot keep men on the land to-day who have invested their life savings on their farms; even although they have spent all their lives on the land, through no fault of their own they are being forced off, as my hon. friend from South Perth said this afternoon. It is all very well to talk loudly about schemes for taking people out of the cities and putting them on the land, but you cannot keep them there. I think the minister is well advised to take the matter into his consideration, and I hope he will consider it for a long time before embarking on a similar scheme. You would never think of spending money to put a man in a law office or to make a doctor of him unless he had somebody behind him financially.
Any fool can be a lawyer.

Perhaps he can; the difficulty is some people seem to think that any fool can be a farmer. If you give a man with some practical experience an acre of land, perhaps he is better off there than wandering homeless in a city. But at the moment any large scheme of land settlement will have just the same chance of success as the soldier settlement scheme had, and it will cost the country just as much money. If you go into such a scheme with your eyes open, with no hope of any return on your investment, I am satisfied; but otherwise for heaven's

sake don't embark on it. Why do we advocate this method of settling on the land people who find themselves in difficulties? I would deprecate anything like the dole, but unfortunately conditions are such in this country today that people cannot be allowed to starve, and perhaps the cheapest way is to grant them direct relief. By the way, I may say that until the government changes its policy perhaps that will have to be done. But the minister is being bombarded this afternoon with requests to go into another land settlement scheme, and I warn him that if he does so he will have just the same results as we had from the soldier land settlement scheme. The minister's idea of advising people who are willing to invest their money in farms is all right, but from my experience in connection with the department I say to the minister that it would be just as well not to open up any discussion about land settlement schemes, because they invariably lead to requests for assistance from all quarters. If we are to give such assistance, let us give it without any hope of ever receiving our money back.

I sympathize with the minister because I have been fighting this battle for a number of years both in and outside the cabinet. subtopic: RAILWAY COMMISSION AND RATE STRUCTURE -SPECLAL COMMODITY RATES

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 44, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: RAILWAY COMMISSION AND RATE STRUCTURE -SPECLAL COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
This is an equalizing freight bill intended to give to the west what we think is due them -the same classification as has been made on the eastern lines through to Fort William. The trouble is that those who fix the rates do not always use good judgment. For instance, they always penalize a commodity that will stand the maximum rate. I have been shipping all my life and have had a

Railway Act
good deal of experience in this regard, and I know that the railroads are sure to get the maximum out of any commodity that can stand it. This necessitates a battle for the rights of the shipper. Take, for example, a carload of silk from Vancouver to New York as against a carload of coal; there is a vast difference in the freight, because they charge whatever the commodity will stand. We argue that one commodity rate should apply to all coarse grains, and we are opposed to the discrimination between the export and domestic rates. We contend that the domestic rate should be brought more into line with the export. The farmers of the prairies no doubt have a low grade grain that could be shipped to the coast for poultry or stock feed if they were given a satisfactory rate, but of course it would have to be lower than the present rate. This would not only furnish a market for the low grade grain which the farmer on the prairie has; it would also help the consumer in British Columbia. The climatic conditions are particularly favourable there for stock and poultry raising and, while things are quiet at the moment,- an enormous business has been done there. But there could have been a good deal more if lower rates had been in effect on all rough commodity freights. There is a regular lumber commodity rate and also a lower rate for slabwood, poles, ties and cordwood. It costs as much to ship a carload of lumber as it does to ship a carload of cordwood or slabs. Why should not a little common sense be used and these rates reduced on coarse grain as well as on wood products? The railroads are looking for business and I think they would find it by adopting these rates. It would help not only themselves but business generally. Vancouver is a port open twelve months m the year, and it is possible that there would be considerable business in poultry exporting if it was possible to obtain feed from the prairies at a satisfactory price. The equalization of the export and domestic rates oh grain would help not only the farmers on the prairies, but the people of British Columbia and throughout Canada as a whole.

subtopic: RAILWAY COMMISSION AND RATE STRUCTURE -SPECLAL COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say in connection with this bill. We have not the bill before us, but from what has been said by the hon. member who introduced this measure we have been able to obtain a fair idea of its provisions. The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Munn) dealt more with commodity rates, but so far as I can understand, it is not intended that this bill shall deal with such rates.
The very important and complicated question of freight rates has been before parliament for some time and has been the subject of discussion throughout the country. I am sorry to say that at times this matter has been injected into the political arena in an effort to make some political gain. It is not my intention to go at length into the history of freight rates. This matter came before parliament over thirty years ago and some hon. members may recall the system then in use for the adjusting of freight rate schedules. Prior to 1903 the railways simply filed their tariffs with the Department of Railways and the railway committee of the privy council either approved or disapproved of such schedules. This system proved to be very unsatisfactory as many of the provinces complained they were being discriminated against and had no voice in the fixing of rates. In 1903 parliament, under the leadership of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, appointed what is known as the Board of Railway Commissioners, designed to function as a court of record and established in the same way as the supreme and exchequer courts. It was to have complete control and authority over all questions relating to the operation of railways, including the charges to be made for the handling of traffic. As I have indicated, it was to function as a judicial body to hear all interested parties, and its decisions were to depend, first, on the evidence submitted, and, second, on a proper appreciation of the evidence in relation to the relief sought. Provision was made for appeals from decisions to the privy council. I think it will be admitted that on the whole this board has proved to be satisfactory. At times there has been criticism, but every section of Canada has been granted the opportunity to appear before the board.
As I understand the present bill, one of its provisions is to add further powers to those already possessed by the railway commission; it is to be given the power to consider matters of trade development and public policy. The objection to this provision is that it would give a political tinge to the railway commission; there would be danger of disturbing its judicial character.
Another provision of the bill is to permit the fixing of rates without a hearing-in other words, to extend the Crowsnest pass agreement west from Fort William to Vancouver. It might be well to recall just what is meant by the Crowsnest pass agreement. This agreement was entered into in 1897 by the Dominion government and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Under its terms the railway agreed
Railway Act

to construct a line through what is known as the Crowsnest pass to Nelson, British Columbia, for which it was to receive a subsidy of $11,000 per mile, or a total of $3,400,000. In return the railroad was to give a rate on grain and flour, from points west of Fort William to Fort William and any point east thereof, of three cents per hundred pounds less than the existing rate. In addition certain reductions were made in the rates on named articles or commodities shipped from the east westward. This agreement remained in force until 1918, when, under the War Measures Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners was given temporary power over the agreement. In 1924 it automatically came into force again, after which an appeal was made to the supreme court with the result that the board was directed to restore the rates provided by the agreement. At the same time the supreme court found in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in its contention that the terms of the agreement applied only to those points which were in existence at the time of the making of the agreement. It is quite apparent that in view of the condition which prevailed as a result of the decision of the supreme court, some action had to be taken; the old agreement had to be either cancelled or extended to take in the other points including the Canadian National.
A large number of people hold the view that since in 1903 we set up a court to deal with this matter, the railway commission, that court, should be given a free hand^ rather than be hampered by any such legislation. In the session of 1925 the government of the day brought in legislation extending the rate under the agreement to other points, including those reached by the Canadian National Railways. I may be pardoned for expressing the opinion that the action of the government of that day was no doubt based on political expediency; a general election was pending, and by leaving the old Crowsnest pass rate agreement in operation the government thought they would be able to draw support from the prairie provinces.
It is very interesting to read the debate on this matter during the session of 1925. It will be noticed that the Conservative members from British Columbia argued that the agreement should be abrogated, or if the government insisted on putting into force legislation extending the agreement, in all fairness it should be extended as far west as Vancouver. Its supporters on the other hand argued that the government was dealing quite fairly with British Columbia, and pointed out that an order in council had just been passed directing the railway commission to make a general

review of freight rates and to provide for their equalization throughout Canada. The government laid special stress on the provision for an appeal to the privy council, where, it was said, justice would surely be meted out. No doubt the order in council was framed with the object of giving the impression that other sections of the dominion would have their grievances adjusted. At this point I desire to quote from the debate. I find that on page 4440 of Hansard of June 18, 1925, the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the present leader of the opposition, in discussing the matter said:
I would say to the house and the country that if this government remains in office it will not take the view of the order in council which my right hon. friend takes-
That is, Mr. Meighen.
-but will regard that order in council as a direction to the railway commission as to how it expects this policy to be worked out, and will see that the policy is W'orked out in accordance with the terms of the order in council. The order in council sets out the government policy. It is a direction to the railway commission to equalize rates. That direction indicates how this government expects this policy of equalization to be worked out. And I would remind hon. members that there remains, as the commission itself well knows, an appeal from the commission to the governor in council with respect to matters of railway rates. This government has stated what its policy is with respect to the equalization of rates, and unless that policy is carried out in accordance with its intention-if this government is in office when the question comes up-and I have not the least doubt it will be-it will take care to see that the policy is carried out in the spirit and intent of the letter as expressed in the order in council itself.
As I have said, great stress was laid on this appeal to the governor in council. Now, the right hon. gentleman's government was in power for the following five years, with the exception of an interruption of a few months, and although an appeal from the decision of the railway commission was taken to the privy council, up to the time of the election of 1930, no decision had been rendered. Having regard to the pledge given at the time, I think it may well be claimed that the Liberal government of that day did not keep faith with the people of Canada, and particularly with the people of British Columbia, in the matter of freight rate adjustments.
During the course of that debate the Conservative members from British Columbia urged the government to abrogate the agreement or extend it to Vancouver. The member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) the other evening said he could not understand why this bill did not have the active support of all members from British Columbia. Well,

Railway Act
the hon. member himself sat in this house during the session of 1925. I have gone very carefully through the debate to which I have referred, but I cannot find that he offered any suggestions to the then government, nor did he support the Conservative members from British Columbia who demanded justice for their province with respect to freight rates. Apparently he was a supporter of the government's legislation and a believer in the policy of that government with respect to the matter as outlined in the order in council. That was his opportunity to serve British Columbia by using his influence with a government that was friendly to him, if he believed, as he does to-day, that that particular legislation was in the interest of British Columbia. Now 'he sees an opportunity to gain a little political kudos out of this matter and is prepared to jump into the boat along with my friend from New Westminster. The people of British Columbia took the promise of the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) very seriously. I remember quite well the striking headlines in the Vancouver press, particularly in the Vancouver Sun. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni still has a copy of that paper on his file. On the front page were large photos of three of the lions of the Liberal party-the Hon. John Oliver, the Hon. Doctor King, and Mr. Jerry McGeer- with this declaration: These are the three men to whom credit is due for what they secured for British Columbia in the way of freight rates, an opportunity of pleading its cause. The cause was pleaded before a friendly and sympathetic government-but still the differential remains.	Time has
wrought great changes; one of those gentlemen has passed to the great beyond, one has been translated to another place, and the third, the $150,000 freight rate advocate, is busy looking for another fat job.
As I have already said, I think the opinion is general that such a complicated matter as freight rates and railway tariffs should be left in the hands of a competent and judicial board, such as we have in the railway commission. I should like again to quote from Hansard of the same date, page 4439, where will be found these remarks by the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the present leader of the opposition:
I have been looking over some of the speeches which I made in western Canada last fall, and which were quoted, in part I think, by the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) in his remarks the. other evening. I notice in speaking on the prairies I intimated very clearly that my view was that the railway
commission was the right body to fix freight rates and should be given a free hand in the matter, When speaking in Vancouver and Victoria I made similar statements.
At that time we had the leader of the opposition arguing that this whole matter should be left in the hands of the railway commission. Then at page 4413 of the same date of Hansard the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) made the following statement:
Admitting therefore, as I do, and as I think all will, that class legislation is bad, that special agreements for the advantage of any one section of the country are bad, and also that the matter of freight rate making should not be given to parliament, we have then to consider, so far as I see the question, how far we should depart in the public interest from the principle that I laid down, that rate making should not be given to parliament but should remain vested in the Board of Railway Commissioners.
At page 4420 we have this further testimony from this same hon. gentleman:
The railway board is charged with the duty of making rates fair and equitable to all. We have set up the board to do that work. Why then not let the board perform that duty? They are infinitely better qualified to make these rates than are members of parliament. If parliament has no confidence in the railway board -and that sentiment has been expressed by some hon. members-then the remedy is not to throw the business of rate-making into this house: the remedy is so to constitute your board that you will have confidence in it.
I think that answers very fully the question which the hon. member brought up the other night in introducing this question.
I have mentioned that the Conservatives also took part in that debate. I shall quote only one. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) at page 4319 of Hansard of June 16, 1925, said:
I have argued in this house and before my own constituents and the people of my province for certain principles which I think should underlie and govern the making of a freight rate structure. I have argued that the fixation of rates is such a complicated problem that it should not be pitchforked into parliament, but rather that it should be dealt with by a competent board, that board in my estimation being the Board of Railway Commissioners.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I think it is the general opinion of all sections of this house and throughout the country that such a complicated matter as freight rates should be left in the hands of an independent judicial tribunal such as the Board of Railway Commissioners. Before this board the railways have the privilege of appearing as well as the people. Any body or individual can appear before the railway board and lay before it
Railway Act

any hardship that may be worked on them through the running of the railways.
I am anxious to support any movement which will bring relief to the farmers of British Columbia and which will help to remove that 21* cents diffei'ential that exists between the domestic and the export rates on grain. I listened very carefully to the hon. gentleman's remarks when he introduced this proposal. I have studied the question very closely, and I have come to the conclusion that the legislation proposed by this bill will not give to the people of our province that which they feel they are justly entitled to. Not only that, but if this bill should become law it would still further tie the hands of the railway board.
There is another objection. There is at the present time an appeal pending before the privy council from the railway commission, and from the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the other day during the debate on this particular question we can take it that this government has been prepared for the last year or year and a half to hear the appeal without delay, but so far the provinces have not been able to arrange a time suitable to all. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, if I thought that by this legislation or any other method justice would be done to the people of Canada and British Columbia would receive what she is entitled to in the matter of the removal of that differential, I should be only too willing to lend my support.

Rideau canal, improvements, $17,000.
Is that canal of any practical service to anybody? If so, let us know; if not, why spend the money? Years ago it may have been some use; what about to-day?
Yes, the Quebec canals are all useful. A great deal of wheat from the prairie provinces passes through them.

Oh, I beg the hon. member's pardon. The Rideau canal is not used for business purposes to any great extent. As my hon. friend knows, it was built in the old days for war purposes, or something of that sort. It is kept open, although very little business passes through it. I should like to refer to the reduction in wages of the men on these canals. I understood the minister's explanation to be that the reduction was a realignment or readjustment of wages to conform to the prevailing rate of wages in the district. I gathered from the minister's explanation that different grades of craftsmanship had been established. Probably the minister is not prepared to go on with this item just now.
Go ahead, but please speak a little louder.

I understand the minister or his department has established first and second class carpenters, blacksmiths, machinists, chauffeurs, engineers, and so on. I was wondering if he would be willing to conform to a ruling which has prevailed in the Department of Labour for a great many years, namely, that there be only one class of craftsmanship. For instance, a carpenter was a man who used the tools of a carpenter)

I was more familiar with this matter a few days ago than I am at the

Supply-Canals
moment, and I am refreshing my memory. They are not all arranged in the two classes, as my hon. friend has suggested. Some types of workmen are divided into two classes. From a hurried observation I notice that there are first and second class carpenters, blacksmiths and cable splicers. Then on the next page of the information I have before me there may be one or two other types of crafstmen divided into the two classes; out of the twenty-five or thirty different types of workers there may be four divided into first and second classes. The rate of wages, however, was established after consultation with the Department of Labour concerning the prevailing rate of wages.

Will not the minister reconsider his position concerning the establishment of different grades? There has been a great deal of trouble in connection with the establishment of wage rates. I can recall that while the Hon. Thomas Crothers was Minister of Labour a ruling was made that a man using the tools of a carpenter should be classed and paid as a carpenter. The reason was that there were contractors working for the government who had to pay the prevailing rate of wages for carpenters. In order to get around that clause in their contracts they established different grades of carpenters. Those men were all doing the same work, but there would be only two or three first class carpenters on a job, and the rest would be second or third. If the establishment of different grades prevails a great deal of trouble will be heaped upon the minister and the government. Therefore I ask the minister to reconsider his view. The change to which I have referred was not made without due consideration, and the result was satisfactory both to the government and to the contractors. In connection with government works contractors file tenders which they believe will secure the work. Immediately they begin to seek ways and means of saving money so that their profits may be greater. Naturally they turn to the item of wages, and make an effort to cut them down. The government will not allow them to cut wages, so they then attempt to establish different grades of labour, first and second class carpenters and so on. That is a vicious method of defeating the fair wage clause, and I am sure the minister does not wish to allow contractors to employ cut-throat methods in connection with their tenders, and attempt to reduce the wages of the workingmen by the establishment of these various grades. The laws laid down governing fair wages do not force any contractor to
keep any particular man employed; the services of an unsatisfactory workman may be dispensed with. On the other hand if a man is engaged as a carpenter he should be paid carpenter's wages.
After long years of experience it has been found necessary to establish only one grade of carpenters, blacksmiths, machinists and craftsmen of all types. I ask the minister to reconsider his view, and to follow the rules of the Department of Labour, the one prevailing since the days of Hon. Thomas Crothers, to the effect that a man using the tools of a carpenter must be paid the wages of a carpenter.

I am afraid I gave my
hon. friend the wrong information. Originally there was an intention to make provision for first and second class carpenters. My hon. friend was one who made objection, and further objections were received from men on the Welland ship canal. The matter was discussed with the Department of Labour, and as a result the provision for second class carpenters was struck out. The result is that there are none. May I add that there have been second class carpenters on the Quebec canals since 1920; whether or not they are retained against the rules of the Department of Labour, I do not know.

I should like to draw the
attention of the minister to the work going on in connection with the Rideau canal. I have no objection to that work, but I do object to being tossed out of my bed during the night because of explosions taking place on the work. I do not want that to happen again. Surely there should be some thought for comfort and convenience of the people.

I do not wish to be unkind to my hon. friend, but in this instance he is in the position in which he so often finds himself in this house. The government is not doing the work; it is being done by the city of Ottawa.

I have a clipping here
from Labour, which is the official organ of the railroad brotherhoods and other international labour organizations. Under date of March 17 it says:
Maintenance workers on Canadian canals have been handed two stiff blows by the Department of Railways and Canals.
It has announced a -wage cut, running as high as 25 per cent and retroactive to February 16, and a new classification that wrill cut further into the workers' depleted pay envelopes.
Is it true that the twenty-five per cent cut in wages was made on the date mentioned, February 16?

There was a cut which
came into effect at about that time. I explained it once before in the house in reply to a question asked by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River. The reason was that there was a reduction in the hours of work just before the last election, while the wages were continued at the same rate per day, which put the men on those canals altogether out of line with the prevailing rate of wages in whatever section was concerned. After consultation with the Department of Labour the prevailing rate was ascertained and these men were merely put on the hourly rate prevailing in the particular section.
Would the minister say the basic rate was cut twenty-five per cent?

I do not know what my
hon. friend means by the basic rate.
The hourly rate.

Yes, that is right; the
hourly rate was cut by 25 per cent, or whatever it was, in order to make the rate the same as the rate paid in those districts by other employers.

Just to keep the record
straight, Mr. Chairman, I may say that though the minister, with his nice smile, says the hours of labour were reduced just before the last election, that was done as part of a permanent policy. It may have been right or wrong, but it was a set policy. The treaty of Versailles, which was signed by Sir Robert Borden on behalf of this country, called for a reduction in the hours of work. In nearly every instance where hours were reduced it will be found that wages or salaries were not interfered with. For instance, when the railway men obtained the -McAdoo award reducing their hours from ten to eight the wages were left as they had been previously, and

when civil servants in Ottawa were put on the eight-hour day salaries and wages were not reduced. The same action was taken in connection with canal employees. When reductions were made in the hours of work, on canals or any other public works, notwithstanding that it was done just before the election it was the intention that salaries and wages would not be reduced in line with the reduction in working time. At the moment I am not complaining because of what the minister has done, but I do want to say it was the intention of the previous government to leave those salaries as they had been. The whole trend in labour circles throughout the world is that hours should be reduced but that the earning power should not be reduced correspondingly. I just make this statement for the information of the minister; this action was not taken because of the election but was part of the policy adopted by the previous government.
I would not for a moment suggest that this was done because of the election; I merely mentioned the date, which happened to be July 16. I am sure it had no connection with the election.

Trent canal, improvements, $133,400.
Would the minister explain this item?

This work is being carried on in connection with the Trent canal, which as my hon. friend knows runs from Trenton to the Georgian bay. There are a number of different items; I have a whole list here. The amount is to provide for plant and channel improvements, structural replacements, rebuilding and concreting of old decaying timber dams, aids to navigation, miscellaneous surveys, investigations and so on. Since 1925 no heavy capital expenditures have been made towards the completion of a through Trent waterway from Trenton to Georgian bay. This is for fairly heavy work in different parts of that canal, which extends for 240 miles.

Practically none.

I think there is a little freight traffic, but it is largely the same type of traffic that is carried on the Rideau canal. There is some tourist traffic, and after all the tourist traffic of the country is one of our big industries. I think there is very,little freight, however.

Is there any fishing up
there ?
I think so.

I am somewhat familiar with the Trent canal; I know that country fairly well, and I think this government should consider very carefully the further expenditure of money on that useless inland waterway. You can sit on the bank for a week and see nothing but an odd gas boat, go up and down the canal. I do not think the expenditure of $100,000 in order to provide a canal for a few fellows with gas boats is justified. I lived in Orillia, close to this canal, for several years and I think it is one of the most miserable failures of all our inland waterways.

While there is no income from the traffic on the canal there are water powers that must be kept up, and we do get an income nearly equal to the amount of this vote. Last year the income was nearly $98,000, and for each of the two previous years it was about $95,000. This income came from lock houses, water powers, land rent, transmission and telephone lines, boat houses and so on. The water powers provide ninety-five per cent of the income, so that the works must be kept up.
Where are the water powers?

I do not know that I can give my hon. friend the exact places, but we are getting the income so I do not suppose the names matter much. With the exception of the vote last year this is the smallest amount to be voted for a number of years. A great deal of money has been spent on this waterway, and my recollection is that for many years in the neighbourhood of $250,000 was voted each year. There has been an agitation up towards Georgian bay to have the canal completely opened to Georgian bay, but that has not been done as yet. There is a good deal of capital expenditure necessary before that is done; it would require $3,000,000 more. But we have no intention at the moment of undertaking that expenditure in view of present financial conditions. The upkeep of the canal is necessary, however, and this expenditure this year, exactly as in past years, is distributed to meet absolute necessities wherever they exist.

The minister has said that
there is no revenue from the canal. That is the fact. Is there any revenue from any of the canals?
No, none except the power revenue.

Would the minister care to
express an opinion on a matter which has been discussed in this house before and which is of some importance, namely, the question whether there should not be revenues from all our canals? Why should 'a private business -and it is almost entirely private business- have free use of canals constructed at the expense of the country? Has the minister thought of the advisability of at least making the canals self-sustaining, even if we get no interest on capital investment?

Tolls were abolished in
1903 by the Laurier government-

That does not make any
difference.

I am not saying this in
order to make any invidious comparison; I am simply stating a fact. Since that time no tolls have been charged on canals in Canada. There are sound arguments that could be advanced in support of the contention that tolls should be charged, but I do not know that it would be advisable at the present time.
This is just the time, when you need the money.

Yes, but it would be to
a large extent a toll upon western wheat, and this commodity is bringing about the lowest price paid in a considerable time. It is true that the Panama canal and the Suez canal charge tolls, and, as I say, there are arguments to support that view. But I do not think I should care to express any definite opinion on the matter at the moment. It is quite open to debate and my hon. friend has good ground for the position he has taken.

I personally brought the
matter up in the house some years ago and it has been brought up by others, and the only reply I have ever heard to the question why tolls should not be charged is that it has always been done this way. I regard that as a very insufficient answer.

So far as tolls on
the Trent canal are concerned, I fear that the revenue would be so small that you could not see it. There are one or two sand barges that go through the canal in the season, but

the toll would be infinitesimal. What I wish to protest against, though, is not only the large vote expended on what is more or less a luxury-a vote of $133,400-but the fact that 1he vote has been increased from the previous year by the sum of $17,000. In the previous year the amount authorized was $116,400, and this year, in face of a curtailment of expenditures generally; a cutting down in the salaries of civil servants by ten per cent; a cutting down in sessional indemnities of members and senators by ten per cent; and a cutting down in the wages of railway employees by more than ten per cent-as we have heard to-night, it is twenty-five per cent-we are launching out on what might be described as a luxurious expenditure. The minister made reference to the tourist traffic. I venture the statement that our tourist traffic is not attracted here by the merits of the Trent canal; the tourists come to see something far more attractive than that. So that an expenditure of $17,000 more this year than was spent last year in a matter of this kind looks to me like extravagance run riot.

With regard to that twenty-five per cent reduction in wages, which went into effect on February 16, is it the intention of the government to add to that reduction the further ten per cent cut made in salaries and wages of civil servants?

It is a matter that we have been discussing, and ordinarily it would have been done without any question whatever. I rather think, frankly, that it will have to be done in fairness to other governmental employees. It is a little unfortunate that the twenty^five iper cent reduction was made so close to the ten per cent proposal, but as a matter of fact when the twenty-five per cent reduction went into effect the ten per cent decrease had not been thought of by the government, so far as I know at any rate. It is true that this should have been done when we first came in, but it was called to my attention by my officers about the time it was put into effect and when I found what I considered was not a reasonable rate, after discussing the matter with the officers of my department and with the Labour department, we put into effect the rates that now prevail. As to the ten per cent, we have been giving a good deal of thought to that, because it does seem rather unfair to the men. But they have this to remember, that for a year and a half they received better wages than men in the same kind of employment in other parts of the country; so that while it appears at the present time to be a severe cut, they had enjoyed that

advantage for over a year. The cheques went out two days ago with the ten per cent taken off. The question is still under consideration, but at the moment it is altogether likely that the ten per cent will remain off.
What pay do these men receive now with the ten per cent off?
Did I understand the minister to say that he was reconsidering his decision in this matter of the ten per cent?

No. I said that the matter was still under consideration, not having been absolutely decided, but I was frank enough to say that I thought the ten per cent would have to remain off in justice to other governmental employees. They will be treated on the same basis.

I can see the minister's point of view, that when a general reduction of ten per cent is being applied all round he should apply it here as well. I can understand why he does not wish to exempt the employees on canals. But I want to point out that the rest of the government employees did not have a twenty-five per cent reduction right on the eve of the ten per cent cut, so that in that regard the canal employees are in a little different position. If the minister will give me his attention-
I am listening to the hon. gentleman.

He takes too much notice of his officers in making these cuts. I say, the rest of the government employees did not suffer a twenty-five per cent cut on the eve of a further ten per cent reduction, so that- these particular employees are now going to suffer to the extent of thirty-five per cent. Even if we admit for the moment that perhaps they had been receiving for a time more than the then prevailing rates of wages, a thirty-five per cent cut is a pretty heavy one.
May I say here-

One moment. As I pointed out the other evening to the Minister of Finance, who agreed with me, if the minister reduces his employees another ten per cent then the contractors in that particular district will have the right to ask the Labour department for a further reduction of ten per cent so far as they are concerned, to bring their employees on a level with the canal employees. And so on down the line. There is no end to it when you are going down, although there is always an end when you

are going up. I repeat, I can see the minister's point of view, but I want him to reconsider the matter. I have no doubt there are many people outside of this House of Commons who would be willing to act as members of parliament for considerably less than S3,600 per year, and there are many who would be willing to accept the job of Minister of Railways at a great deal less than the minister is receiving at the present time. union will be receiving different rates of pay, the one rate ten per cent below the other. I draw this aspect of the matter to the attention of the minister, as I do not think the government took it seriously into consideration when it adopted the general cut.

The government took
advantage of the depression in order to reduce its own rates by twenty-five per cent, and now it proposes to make a further cut. This will be setting an example to outside employers to reduce again their rates of pay by ten per cent.

When Bill No. 19, which provides for the ten per cent cut, was introduced by the Prime Minister for the Minister of Finance, such a case as this was referred to. The Prime Minister was asked if some men who had recently had their wages cut would receive a further cut of ten per cent, and he answered to the effect that there was a special provision in the bill to take care of such cases. The treasury board may make regulations.-
(b) determining in any case of doubt the amount to be treated as the amount of compensation of any member of the public service of Canada for the purposes of this act.
That subsection was to take care of just such cases as we have been discussing this evening. I suggest to the minister that all he has to do is to take advantage of the procedure provided by that subsection and thus fulfil the assurances given by the Prime Minister.

The matter is not absolutely decided, and I shall agree to give it further consideration, although I shall not go any further than that at the moment. Don't you think the government ought to be a model employer of labour?
Yes, and I think we are.
Two cuts of twenty-five per cent?
That is not fair.

One of twenty-five and one
of ten per cent.

My hon. friend thought that plenty of people would be willing to become members of parliament at $3,600 a year.
